slides.title: Title Slide
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on Understanding **APIs**.
slides.image_prompt: Title Slide

slides.title: Learning Objectives Slide
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn,

• Define what an **API** is and its role in modern applications.
• Explain how **APIs** facilitate communication between applications and **AI** models.
• Identify the importance of **API** keys for authentication and access control.
• Illustrate the end-to-end process of sending requests and receiving **AI**-generated responses via an **API**.
slides.image_prompt: Learning Objectives Slide

slides.title: System Requirements Slide
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.
slides.image_prompt: System Requirements Slide

slides.title: Pre-requisite Slide
slides.narration:
To follow this tutorial, you should have a basic understanding of how software applications interact and general computing concepts.
No coding needed.
slides.image_prompt: Pre-requisite Slide

slides.title: What is an API?
slides.narration:
Let's begin by understanding what an **API** is.
**API** stands for Application Programming Interface.
It's a foundational concept in modern software.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: What is an API?

slides.title: API: The Digital Messenger
slides.narration:
Think of an **API** as a digital messenger.
It allows different software applications to talk to each other.
It acts as an intermediary, handling requests and responses.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing API as a digital messenger facilitating communication

slides.title: Why APIs are Essential
slides.narration:
Why are **APIs** essential?
They enable seamless communication and integration.
Without them, different software systems would operate in isolation.
This means no sharing data or functionalities easily.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing interconnected software systems vs isolated ones

slides.title: API as a Connector
slides.narration:
With that understanding, let's explore an analogy.
Imagine an **API** as a bridge or a connector.
It links various software components together.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: API as a Connector

slides.title: The Request-Response Flow
slides.narration:
An **API** works on a request-response flow.
One application sends a request to the **API**.
The **API** then delivers this request to another application.
Finally, it brings the response back to the first application.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing request-response flow between two applications via an API

slides.title: Connecting Applications to AI Models
slides.narration:
This request-response flow is crucial for **AI**.
**APIs** are the conduit for applications to interact with powerful **AI** models.
They allow apps to send data to an **AI** model.
And then receive the **AI**-generated output.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing application sending data to an AI model via an API and receiving output

slides.title: Prompts as API Inputs
slides.narration:
Now, let's talk about **prompts**.
How do we tell an **AI** model what we want?
We send them as inputs through the **API**.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: Prompts as API Inputs

slides.title: Understanding Prompts in API Calls
slides.narration:
When you type a question for **ChatGPT** or **Gemini**,
that's a **prompt**.
In an **API** call, a **prompt** is part of the request payload.
It's the instruction or query for the **AI** model.
slides.image_prompt: Person at laptop, typing a prompt into a chat interface

slides.title: Basic API Call with a Simple Prompt
slides.narration:
Let's see a basic example.
Imagine an application asking an **AI** model:
'Tell me a fun fact about space.'
This simple sentence is the **prompt** in our **API** request.
See how direct and clear it is?
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Tell me a fun fact about space.'...

slides.title: API Call with a Structured Prompt
slides.narration:
But we can make our **prompts** even better.
Look at this improved example.
Here, the **prompt** is structured with roles.
For instance, 'You are a helpful assistant. Explain **APIs** simply.'
This guides the **AI** for a more precise response.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'You are a helpful assistant. Explain APIs simply.'...

slides.title: Impact of Prompt Structure on API Responses
slides.narration:
Now, let's compare the impact.
A simple **prompt** might give a general answer.
But a structured **prompt** leads to a more relevant and specific **AI**-generated response.
It's like giving clear instructions versus vague ones.
See the difference in output quality?
slides.image_prompt: Side-by-side: vague prompt output vs improved prompt output

slides.title: API Keys and Security
slides.narration:
Moving on, let's discuss security.
How do we ensure only authorized users access **APIs**?
This is where **API** keys come in.
They are a critical component for securing **API** services.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: API Keys and Security

slides.title: What are API Keys?
slides.narration:
What exactly are **API** keys?
An **API** key is a unique identifier.
It's a secret token that authenticates your application.
It tells the **API** server who is making the request.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing API key as a digital key or token

slides.title: Authentication and Access Control
slides.narration:
**API** keys are crucial for authentication.
They verify your identity when you access an **API**.
They also control your access permissions.
This means you can only use the functionalities you are allowed to.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing lock and key icon representing authentication and access control

slides.title: Best Practices for API Key Management
slides.narration:
Managing **API** keys securely is vital.
Always keep your **API** keys confidential.
Never embed them directly in client-side code.
Use environment variables or secure vaults for storage.
This prevents unauthorized access to your services.
slides.image_prompt: Person at laptop, securing a digital key or token

slides.title: The API Request-Response Lifecycle
slides.narration:
Now, let's put it all together.
We will outline the complete **API** request-response lifecycle.
This shows the end-to-end interaction.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: The API Request-Response Lifecycle

slides.title: Making an API Request
slides.narration:
First, an application formulates a request.
It includes the **prompt** and your **API** key.
This request is sent to a specific **API** endpoint.
Think of an endpoint as a specific address for a service.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing application sending a request with prompt and API key to an API endpoint

slides.title: Processing the AI Response
slides.narration:
Once the **AI** model processes the request,
it sends back a response.
The application receives this data through the **API**.
It then interprets and uses the **AI**-generated output.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing AI model processing request and sending response back to application via API

slides.title: End-to-End API Interaction Example
slides.narration:
Let's walk through an end-to-end example.
An application wants to generate an image from text.
It sends a **prompt** like 'A cat in space' to an **AI** image generation **API**.
With the correct **API** key, the **AI** processes it.
Then, the **API** returns the generated image to the application.
This completes the full interaction cycle.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'A cat in space'... AI generating response on screen

slides.title: Summary Slide
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined what an **API** is and its role as a digital messenger.
We saw how **APIs** connect applications to **AI** models.
We understood that **prompts** are inputs sent through **APIs**.
And we highlighted the importance of **API** keys for security and access.
Finally, we outlined the complete request-response lifecycle.
slides.image_prompt: Summary Slide
